title: Three Monks Have No Water to Drink
text:
A Chinese saying runs: one monk carries water by himself, two monks carry water together, three monks have no water to drink. The story behind it goes like this.

A young monk lived alone in a small temple on a hill. Each day he carried two buckets on a shoulder pole down to the river and back, filled the water jar, and tended the temple. Then a second monk arrived. Neither wanted to do more than the other, so they carried a single bucket between them, the pole across both their shoulders, each making sure the bucket hung exactly in the middle.

Then a third monk came. Now nobody would go. Each waited for one of the others, and each thought the job belonged to someone else. The water jar sat empty, and the three monks grew thirsty and sullen, reading their scriptures and ignoring one another.

In the well-known Chinese animated film of 1980 based on the saying, a mouse knocks over a candle one night and the temple catches fire. The three monks run for buckets, form a chain and put the fire out together. Afterward they build a pulley so the water comes up the hill with no argument over who carries it.
lesson: When a task belongs to everyone, it can end up belonging to no one. Assign clear responsibility, or design the work so that sharing it is natural.
source: Chinese folk proverb; Three Monks (San ge heshang), Shanghai Animation Film Studio, 1980
caveat: The proverb is traditional, while the fire and the pulley come from the 1980 film version.
